stories.headline: Cyclone Akvan hits early potato cultivation in Bengal
stories.title: Cyclone Akvan hits early potato cultivation in Bengal
stories.summary: Sowing to be delayed by two weeks, may affect early seeding varieties which account for 10% of total output
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Sowing of potatoes is likely to be delayed by around two weeks in West Bengal, the country’s second-largest grower, due to heavy rain triggered by Cyclone Akvan.
Cultivation of early varieties is feared to be severely hit.
The State may see a fall in total area under potato cultivation in the 2026-27 season.
Cyclone Akvan made landfall near Gopalpur in neighbouring Odisha last week, bringing heavy rain across southern West Bengal and impacting major potato-growing districts.
“Heavy rainfall wreaked havoc in areas where seeds for early varieties had been sown.
In most places, seedbeds may be impacted due to waterlogging, causing a major hit to cultivation,” Patit Paban De, senior member, West Bengal Cold Storage Association, told businessline.

Although early varieties account for only around 10 per cent of Bengal’s total potato production, damage caused by the cyclone is likely to hit farmers financially, leading to a shrinkage in total area.
Hooghly, Purba Bardhaman and Paschim Medinipur in South Bengal are the three largest potato-growing districts in the State.
“Farmers will take a major financial hit due to damage to early varieties.
That will reduce their capacity to cultivate larger areas compared with last year.
Moreover, sowing is likely to be delayed by around two weeks as fields are completely underwater,” said De.
Farmers in the three districts have been unable to harvest mature Aman paddy due to waterlogging.

stories.headline: Union Minister Sarbananda Sonowal slams Congress for doubting Election Commission
stories.title: Union Minister Sarbananda Sonowal slams Congress for doubting Election Commission
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: DIBRUGARH: Union Minister of Ports, Shipping & Waterways (MoPSW), Sarbananda Sonowal criticised the Congress for repeatedly questioning the credibility of the Election Commission and democratic institutions, saying such political conduct undermines public confidence in the country's democratic framework.

Speaking at the Prabuddha Nagarik Sabha, organised by the civil society of Dibrugarh, Sonowal said political differences were a natural part of democracy, but political interests should not take precedence over the credibility and dignity of constitutional institutions.
"Every political party has a responsibility to uphold respect and confidence in the country's constitutional and democratic institutions, including the Election Commission.

Differences of opinion are natural in a democracy, but safeguarding the dignity of our democratic system and the credibility of its institutions, above narrow political interests, is a collective duty," Sonowal said.

Sarbananda Sonowal also highlighted the importance of an informed and responsible citizenry in enhancing democracy, promoting social development, and contributing to nation-building during his interactions with notable individuals from various fields.

Sonowal said India's emergence as one of the world's fastest-growing economies reflected the country's development journey under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, guided by the vision of Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas, Sabka Vishwas and Sabka Prayas.
He called for active participation and cooperation from all sections of society to accelerate the country's progress.
"Nation-building is not the responsibility of the government alone; it is a collective responsibility of every citizen.
The strength of our democracy lies in the awareness, active participation and sense of duty of its citizens.
As we move towards Amrit Kaal 2047, we must work together to build a strong, self-reliant and prosperous India," Sonowal said.

Referring to Assam's history, identity and the rights of its indigenous communities, he said protecting the state's language, culture, heritage and the interests of its people was a collective responsibility.
He described the issue of illegal foreign nationals as a significant concern for Assam and stressed the need for appropriate action in accordance with the law and constitutional provisions.

stories.headline: PT Usha gets relief in IOA election row as Delhi High Court rejects rival faction's petition
stories.title: PT Usha gets relief in IOA election row as Delhi High Court rejects rival faction's petition
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: PT Usha has cleared another hurdle in her bid for a second term as IOA president after the Delhi High Court dismissed a challenge to her inclusion in the electoral roll.
Here's why her nomination through the Ice Hockey Association became controversial.
New Delhi: The Delhi High Court has dismissed a petition challenging the inclusion of former Indian athlete PT Usha in the voter list for the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) elections.

The Ice Hockey Association of India (IHAI) had nominated Usha as its representative to the IOA General Assembly after she failed to secure election under the Sportspersons of Outstanding Merit (SOM) category.
The petition was filed by Kunsang Namgyal, representing a rival faction of the Ice Hockey Association.
The faction questioned Usha's eligibility, arguing that she was not a member of the federation and therefore could not be nominated as its representative.
The nomination had been made by the faction led by IHAI president Gurpreet Singh Bakshi.
With the High Court dismissing the challenge, the legal obstacle to Usha submitting her nomination papers for the IOA elections has been removed.
The nomination process is scheduled to run from November 22 to 24.

The dispute centres on whether Usha could represent the Ice Hockey Association of India in the IOA General Assembly despite not being elected under the category reserved for sportspersons with outstanding achievements.
Usha had contested for a place among the four female Sportspersons of Outstanding Merit but failed to secure a position.

stories.headline: How India is rolling out the red carpet for the big, fat wedding
stories.title: How India is rolling out the red carpet for the big, fat wedding
stories.summary: Europe was a serious contender when Kinjal Shah was planning her wedding, scheduled for March 2027. Her fiancé’s immediate family lived in the US, and it made sense to bring the two sides together there for a function with 100 guests representing the bride and groom. Shah, though, was keen on a traditional Indian wedding, rooted in the country’s culture.“I wanted a maximal Indian wedding, with all the rituals, outfits and ceremonies. I wanted that authenticity, and I managed to convince my fiancé about it,” she tells Forbes India.Shah chose Udaipur because its palaces and heritage hotels offered the royal setting she had imagined. Also, its network of local vendors made the many moving parts of a wedding easier to organise. “You have several options for each requirement. If you need something, you can find multiple vendors instead of having to arrange everything from distant cities,” the wedding planner explains.Also Read: Why luxury's biggest bet on India might be its costliest mistake A San Francisco-based couple brought their closest friends and family to Fairmont Jaipur for their wedding. Photo by The Wedding FilesShah’s is not an isolated case. Indians are increasingly warming up to a location within the country for their big day. And the government is leaving no stone unturned to pursue wealthy Indians, be it locals or NRIs, to keep their wedding spending at home.It has launched initiatives like ‘Wed in India’ and ‘India says I do’ to ensure that NRIs and foreign couples consider the country as a wedding destination. In his ‘Mann Ki Baat’ broadcast in November 2023, Prime Minister Narendra Modi urged wealthy families to consider hosting weddings in India, which laid the foundation for ‘Wed in India’. The Ministry of Tourism had already launched its ‘India Says I Do’ campaign in August 2023, aimed at showcasing the country’s palaces, heritage monuments, beaches, mountains and temples to couples around the world. An Indian wedding taking place at Taj Gorbandh Palace in Jaisalmer in February. Photo by Raabta by Shrey BhagatBoost to economyWhen affluent Indian families take their weddings abroad, much of the money spent on hotels, venues, entertainment and hospitality leaves the economy with them. As destination weddings take place in India, guests spend at restaurants, on shopping and sightseeing. People who travel from overseas extend their stay and explore other locations, spreading the benefit. Devanshi Patel, founder of Shreem Events, points to a chain in Udaipur—a place with high underemployment—where a wedding creates work for florists, fabricators, technicians, folk dancers, musicians, photographers and make-up artists. “If this kind of money, which otherwise goes outside India, stays in India, it’s obviously going to bring the country into the top charts of the wedding industry,” she says.Amrit Arora, founder of The Wedding Files, a wedding photography service, explains that a wedding brings together a network of professionals. “During the pandemic, when weddings were disrupted, we saw how that disruption affected businesses across this ecosystem. The return of celebrations reinforced how many livelihoods depend on the wedding industry functioning well,” he says.States also acknowledge how destination weddings can power local ecosystems. “They undoubtedly create opportunities for local vendors and service providers, while encouraging guests to extend their stays and explore the destination,” says Kedar Naik, director of tourism, Goa.If keeping Indian weddings at home aims at retaining domestic expenditure, bringing foreign weddings to India is about attracting new spending from NRIs and couples who may otherwise choose places such as Thailand, the UAE or Europe.“About 25 percent of the world’s weddings take place in India. The ministry is developing a national wedding tourism digital database, issuing a standard format to obtain destination information covering event capacity, accommodation, facilities, etc,” says a senior official from the tourism ministry on condition of anonymity.Also Read: An ode to love: The big, fat Indian wedding is back with a bangWow for VowsIndia, the stakeholders believe, has the right ingredients for hosting intimate weddings. It’s just that there is a need for making a noise about it.Chetan Vohra, chairperson of FICCI’s Wed in India taskforce, and chairman and managing director of WeddingLine, a wedding planning company, says: “Wed in India is an obvious extension of Incredible India. We’ve done wildlife and medical tourism, and a whole lot more, but there was never a focus on weddings and the industry is massive.”His taskforce works with state governments to identify what is needed to support destination weddings [in India] and wedding tourism. “The idea is to give states the leverage to realise what they need to do to boost wedding tourism, bring everybody up to a certain level, and then unleash an aggressive international campaign saying that all of India is ready to host weddings,” Vohra tells Forbes India. “We have culture, tradition, monuments, temples, beaches, mountains, everything that the world can offer on one canvas.”Several states, especially the ones known as popular wedding destinations, are already taking the lead in this regard. Naik of the Goa government says the coastal state is contributing to India’s broader ambition by coordinating closely with the stakeholders.“Through destination marketing, participation on tourism platforms and engagement with industry stakeholders, we continue to showcase our strengths to wider audiences.By combining quality hospitality with cultural authenticity and local experiences, we can elevate our share,” he says.Desi vs ForeignOne of the biggest and most-talked-about functions that put India in the spotlight as a wedding destination was the Anant Ambani-Radhika Merchant marriage in 2024. The grandeur and scale of the months-long celebrations—from pre-wedding festivities in Jamnagar that included performances by celebrities like Rihanna and Katy Perry, to the final ceremonies in Mumbai—changed the way India’s wedding industry was perceived globally.Also Read: Raj Mantena: The low-profile tycoon behind the viral Udaipur wedding“Wherever we travelled internationally, the first thing anybody would talk about was the Ambani wedding,” says Madhulika Mathur, co-founder and director of WeddingSutra, a bridal media and wedding planning platform. “Some of the high-profile weddings in India are now being discussed among the movers and shakers around the world.”Global attention, though, does not automatically translate into foreign bookings, and the Ambani wedding is not a template every family can replicate. Other factors such as rising hotel costs and the geopolitical situation are also issues that compel people to reconsider hosting their wedding in the country.“India is not a viable destination as of now. It might be frightfully expensive. There has been a 25 to 30 percent increase in hotel prices, maybe more in some places. Our biggest challenge is to get everybody to understand that it has to be made a viable destination,” says Vohra.According to Anjali Tolani, vice president of celebrations at Tamarind Global, a wedding planning company, beyond the destination, expenses related to accommodation, food and beverage, décor and production, entertainment, transportation and guest logistics are also evaluated before making a final decision. “When these components are assessed together, a destination that initially appears more affordable may not necessarily offer better value. An alternative location may allow a family to achieve a more ambitious experience within the same budget,” she says.Foreign locations also have an edge when it comes to the ease of dealing with the government for allowances and permissions.“Permissions and sign-offs make it a little tedious to have a wedding in India,” says Kavneet Sethi, founder of The Wedding Galore, a Thailand-based company which plans Indian weddings. “In Thailand, it’s smooth sailing. You come to the property, see it, like it, sign a deal and that’s it,” she continues, adding that Thai tourism authorities offer incentives and do everything to attract Indian families for a wedding there.Agrees Patel of Shreem Events, who is also a part of the Wed in India campaign. “Internationally, they give you a blanket permission,” she says. “In India, there will be a music licence, alcohol licence, venue licence, police permission, gram panchayat licence, beach licence. It just doesn’t end.”The ease of execution must become as important as the destination’s appeal, according to Tolani. “The experience of planning and delivering a largescale celebration can still be considerably more complex than it needs to be.” So, to compete with Thailand, India needs to learn how the country makes it easier to have a wedding there. The official quoted earlier says the tourism ministry aims to establish simplified approval mechanisms and streamline, in particular, GST-related and music licensing-related issues, by December.‘I Do’ in IndiaDespite the bottlenecks and hurdles, high net-worth individuals (HNI) and ultra-high net-worth individuals (UHNI) are opting for India to host weddings. Planners call this a market shaped by several forces at once: The government’s message, new venue supply and the West Asia crisis.Monil Shah, founder and CEO of Kkings Events, talks about the impact of geopolitics. He says he knows of three weddings that were scheduled to be held in the Middle East but were shifted to India this year because the families and guests did not want to deal with uncertainty. Another couple who initially wanted to marry inAlUla in Saudi Arabia eventually chose Adiyogi in Tamil Nadu. “A strategy was built around it, and they were guided to push something in India instead,” he says.Patel has dealt with multiple instances of weddings being shifted from an overseas location to India. One of her clients changed the destination from Abu Dhabi to Rishikesh, while another wedding planned in Sri Lanka moved to the family’s hometown of Ahmedabad, turning a three-day celebration into a nine-day event. “Families want greater certainty and do not want to expose their guests to travel-related risks,” she says.According to Tolani, for NRIs, a wedding in India is much more than a celebration. “It is an opportunity to reconnect with their roots, bring extended families together and share their heritage with a wider circle of friends, including those who may be experiencing India for the first time.”For many affluent families, a luxury Indian wedding means celebrations over two to three days, sometimes even longer. The rituals are central, connecting the festivities to family, faith and regional culture.Mathur tells Forbes India that the emphasis on personalisation has made luxury Indian weddings more labour-intensive than ever. There are florists, fabricators, musicians, technicians and hospitality teams who collaborate with planners to create an experience.A 2025-26 report by WedMeGood, a digital wedding planning platform, puts the average Indian wedding budget at ₹39.5 lakh, up 8 percent from the previous year. The average budget for a destination wedding in India, in contrast, was ₹58 lakh. More than 60 percent of weddings that cost ₹1 crore or more were held away from home, while 89 percent of destination weddings took place within India.Before Covid, 400 to 600 guests were common in Indian weddings, but that number fell during the pandemic, at times due to government regulations on social gatherings; in 2025, weddings with 600 to 800 guests were again being hosted, with budgets averaging ₹15 crore to ₹20 crore among Kkings Events’ Shah’s clientele. “The Covid phase opened a new segment of intimate weddings, where the spend was big, around ₹5 crore, but only with 100 people,” he says. “The experience was much larger for them. Both segments—intimate and large—are now doing well.”The hotel industry is witness to the change on ground. Nivedan Kukreti, general manager, Taj Corbett Resort, says they have seen an increase in inquiries and bookings from NRIs over the last few years. “Many overseas families are rediscovering India as a wedding destination because it offers something incredibly unique. While costs have certainly risen across the hospitality industry, we have not seen a significant impact on the appetite for luxury weddings,” he says.The luxury market in India may be smaller by volume, but it is disproportionately large in footprint. WeddingSutra’s Annual Luxury and Destination Weddings Survey 2026 found that around 50 percent of UHNIs choose destination celebrations for at least a pre- or post-wedding event, compared with 12 percent of HNIs. And some venues are more favoured than the others.Melting Pot of cultureRajasthan remains the clearest expression of the luxury proposition. Udaipur, Jaipur, Jodhpur and Jaisalmer offer palace hotels, heritage, architecture and dramatic landscapes. “It’s not just the palaces,” Shah says. “The cultural heritage is visible throughout the city.”But the popularity has created a capacity problem. A survey by WeddingSutra, a digital media and wedding planning brand, found that several of Udaipur’s top palace properties are now largely accessible only to UHNIs in peak season, with Jaipur increasingly seen as a cheaper alternative outside the peak period. Shah of Kkings Events reveals that a hotel charged ₹30,000 for bed and breakfast one year and ₹65,000 the next. “A 100 percent increase in a year is unreal,” he says. “It is only because the volume of weddings has increased while the supply is low… that is inflating prices.”If Rajasthan offers heritage, Goa offers a vibe. “With its premium beachfront resorts, luxury hotels, heritage properties, diverse cuisine and established hospitality ecosystem, Goa offers a range of settings for celebrations,” says Naik.Demand is also calendar-bound in India, says Mathur, mainly between mid-January and early May, with February particularly busy.But India cannot depend on Rajasthan or Goa alone. Dehradun and Kerala remain popular, while Kochi, Mahabalipuram, Coorg, Alibaug and Karjat are gaining attention. The WeddingSutra survey also lists Bekal, Amritsar, Rishikesh, Mussoorie, Ramnagar, Agra and Sawai Madhopur among places seeing stronger demand, helped by better connectivity and new four- and five-star hotels.Also Read: Quiet luxury in India: Elites embrace global trend, redefining it on their own termsShah sees spiritual weddings as the next frontier, in places such as Ayodhya, Varanasi, Dwarka, Madurai, Rishikesh, Pushkar, Rameshwaram, Ujjain and Maheshwar. “The format is a small, intimate celebration with closest family members at a location related to spirituality, and somewhere nearby, a grand celebration with the larger audience,” he says.While Thailand offers a lesson in packaging a destination, Sethi concedes that weddings from India in the country have eased, partly because of the government’s call to host at home, but NRI weddings continue. She estimates a typical luxury budget for a 250-person, two-to-three-day wedding in Thailand at around ₹3 crore. Patel puts a lavish 200-person wedding in Udaipur at ₹5-10 crore, against ₹1-4 crore in Khao Lak, Phuket or Bali. Guests gather at a wedding reception at Umaid Bhawan Palace in Jodhpur, Rajasthan. Photo by Olivier Polet / Corbis via Getty ImagesBeyond the weddingAside from the direct wedding economy, a grand Indian wedding also impacts the peripheral industries. Intra-city travel is one such big opportunity. Aman Naagar, managing director of Avis India, which offers chauffeur-driven car services, says a wedding with 200 to 300 guests can require 30 to 50 vehicles. “Even a mid-sized wedding means well over 100 days of paid work for drivers,” he says. “That’s before you count the coordinators on the ground and the fleet owners who supply the vehicles.”During peak season, in Jaipur or Udaipur, several weddings can overlap. “Those are the weeks when local operators are fully booked, and many of them earn a big share of their annual business in those few months,” he adds.That said, there is still more work to be done in positioning India as one of the most coveted choices for weddings. Rising hotel prices, limited rooms, seasonal demand and uneven infrastructure persist, while Thailand and the UAE compete on predictable logistics and strong ecosystems. “The opportunity is immense, but continued investment in infrastructure will be critical,” Kukreti says.Vohra, though, is optimistic. “Given India’s history of hospitality, I think we are definitely on a path to becoming one of the top two or three wedding destinations in the world,” he says. “The number of jobs we give, the employment that goes out, the taxes we contribute with and the revenue we generate are tremendous. We need a lot more to happen, including the government giving us proper industry status.”Tolani says the government’s efforts are necessary; however, sustained success will depend on translating that intent into measurable improvements on ground. “India does not need to compete solely on grandeur or heritage. It needs to compete on a complete proposition. A globally competitive wedding destination combines an extraordinary setting with ease of access, regulatory clarity, service consistency and value,” she says.The government and stakeholders have rolled out the red carpet. It’s just a matter of time before the wedding bells start ringing louder in the country. “India has great infrastructure, great flexibility with weddings, great promotions and great tourism support to build on. If India decides to make that mark globally, it can do it,” says Patel.

According to Anjali Tolani, vice president of celebrations at Tamarind Global, a wedding planning company, beyond the destination, expenses related to accommodation, food and beverage, décor and production, entertainment, transportation and guest logistics are also evaluated before making a final decision.
“When these components are assessed together, a destination that initially appears more affordable may not necessarily offer better value.

Foreign locations also have an edge when it comes to the ease of dealing with the government for allowances and permissions.

“In Thailand, it’s smooth sailing.

You come to the property, see it, like it, sign a deal and that’s it,” she continues, adding that Thai tourism authorities offer incentives and do everything to attract Indian families for a wedding there.
Agrees Patel of Shreem Events, who is also a part of the Wed in India campaign.
“Internationally, they give you a blanket permission,” she says.
“In India, there will be a music licence, alcohol licence, venue licence, police permission, gram panchayat licence, beach licence.
It just doesn’t end.” The ease of execution must become as important as the destination’s appeal, according to Tolani.

“The experience of planning and delivering a largescale celebration can still be considerably more complex than it needs to be.” So, to compete with Thailand, India needs to learn how the country makes it easier to have a wedding there.

Despite the bottlenecks and hurdles, high net-worth individuals (HNI) and ultra-high net-worth individuals (UHNI) are opting for India to host weddings.
Planners call this a market shaped by several forces at once: The government’s message, new venue supply and the West Asia crisis.
Monil Shah, founder and CEO of Kkings Events, talks about the impact of geopolitics.
He says he knows of three weddings that were scheduled to be held in the Middle East but were shifted to India this year because the families and guests did not want to deal with uncertainty.
Another couple who initially wanted to marry inAlUla in Saudi Arabia eventually chose Adiyogi in Tamil Nadu.
“A strategy was built around it, and they were guided to push something in India instead,” he says.
Patel has dealt with multiple instances of weddings being shifted from an overseas location to India.

One of her clients changed the destination from Abu Dhabi to Rishikesh, while another wedding planned in Sri Lanka moved to the family’s hometown of Ahmedabad, turning a three-day celebration into a nine-day event.
“Families want greater certainty and do not want to expose their guests to travel-related risks,” she says.
According to Tolani, for NRIs, a wedding in India is much more than a celebration.

“It is an opportunity to reconnect with their roots, bring extended families together and share their heritage with a wider circle of friends, including those who may be experiencing India for the first time.” For many affluent families, a luxury Indian wedding means celebrations over two to three days, sometimes even longer.
The rituals are central, connecting the festivities to family, faith and regional culture.
Mathur tells Forbes India that the emphasis on personalisation has made luxury Indian weddings more labour-intensive than ever.
There are florists, fabricators, musicians, technicians and hospitality teams who collaborate with planners to create an experience.
A 2025-26 report by WedMeGood, a digital wedding planning platform, puts the average Indian wedding budget at ₹39.5 lakh, up 8 percent from the previous year.
The average budget for a destination wedding in India, in contrast, was ₹58 lakh.

Before Covid, 400 to 600 guests were common in Indian weddings, but that number fell during the pandemic, at times due to government regulations on social gatherings; in 2025, weddings with 600 to 800 guests were again being hosted, with budgets averaging ₹15 crore to ₹20 crore among Kkings Events’ Shah’s clientele.
“The Covid phase opened a new segment of intimate weddings, where the spend was big, around ₹5 crore, but only with 100 people,” he says.
“The experience was much larger for them.
Both segments—intimate and large—are now doing well.” The hotel industry is witness to the change on ground.
Nivedan Kukreti, general manager, Taj Corbett Resort, says they have seen an increase in inquiries and bookings from NRIs over the last few years.
“Many overseas families are rediscovering India as a wedding destination because it offers something incredibly unique.
While costs have certainly risen across the hospitality industry, we have not seen a significant impact on the appetite for luxury weddings,” he says.
The luxury market in India may be smaller by volume, but it is disproportionately large in footprint.
Wedding.
And some venues are more favoured than the others.
Melting Pot of cultureRajasthan remains the clearest expression of the luxury proposition.
Udaipur, Jaipur, Jodhpur and Jaisalmer offer palace hotels, heritage, architecture and dramatic landscapes.
“It’s not just the palaces,” Shah says.
“The cultural heritage is visible throughout the city.” But the popularity has created a capacity problem.

A survey by WeddingSutra, a digital media and wedding planning brand, found that several of Udaipur’s top palace properties are now largely accessible only to UHNIs in peak season, with Jaipur increasingly seen as a cheaper alternative outside the peak period.
Shah of Kkings Events reveals that a hotel charged ₹30,000 for bed and breakfast one year and ₹65,000 the next.

Demand is also calendar-bound in India, says Mathur, mainly between mid-January and early May, with February particularly busy.
But India cannot depend on Rajasthan or Goa alone.
Dehradun and Kerala remain popular, while Kochi, Mahabalipuram, Coorg, Alibaug and Karjat are gaining attention.

The WeddingSutra survey also lists Bekal, Amritsar, Rishikesh, Mussoorie, Ramnagar, Agra and Sawai Madhopur among places seeing stronger demand, helped by better connectivity and new four- and five-star hotels.
Shah sees spiritual weddings as the next frontier, in places such as Ayodhya, Varanasi, Dwarka, Madurai, Rishikesh, Pushkar, Rameshwaram, Ujjain and Maheshwar.
“The format is a small, intimate celebration with closest family members at a location related to spirituality, and somewhere nearby, a grand celebration with the larger audience,” he says.

Patel puts a lavish 200-person wedding in Udaipur at ₹5-10 crore, against ₹1-4 crore in Khao Lak, Phuket or Bali.

Rising hotel prices, limited rooms, seasonal demand and uneven infrastructure persist, while Thailand and the UAE compete on predictable logistics and strong ecosystems.
“The opportunity is immense, but continued investment in infrastructure will be critical,” Kukreti says.

A globally competitive wedding destination combines an extraordinary setting with ease of access, regulatory clarity, service consistency and value,” she says.
The government and stakeholders have rolled out the red carpet.
It’s just a matter of time before the wedding bells start ringing louder in the country.
“India has great infrastructure, great flexibility with weddings, great promotions and great tourism support to build on.
If India decides to make that mark globally, it can do it,” says Patel.

stories.summary: Mumbai, Nov 23 : Indian equity benchmarks snapped a two-session winning streak on Monday, with the Sensex and Nifty posting sharp losses as heavy selling in metal, banking and financial stocks weighed on investor sentiment. The Sensex plunged 1,483.72 points, or 1.77 per cent, to close at 82,435.99, while the Nifty dropped 450.95 points, or 1.75 per cent, to settle at 25,349.65. The decline was led by metal and financial counters, with Tata Steel, Axis Bank and HDFC Bank emerging among the top laggards on the Nifty index. Selling pressure was also visible across the broader market. The Nifty MidCap 100 index fell 1.01 per cent, while the Nifty SmallCap 100 index declined 0.66 per cent. Among sectoral indices, Nifty Metal was the worst performer of the day as investors pared exposure to commodity-linked shares. Banking and financial stocks also remained under pressure, dragging down the Nifty Bank, Nifty PSU Bank, Nifty Financial Services and Nifty Private Bank indices. Auto shares joined the broader market decline, with the Nifty Auto index ending lower. In contrast, information technology stocks bucked the broader downturn. The Nifty IT index gained about 2 per cent. Market experts said that the sharp fall in the benchmarks reflected broad-based weakness across sectors, with investors booking profits after the market's recent rally and rotating into select technology stocks. "Last week’s late global sell-off, triggered by concerns over an AI bubble and tighter US monetary policy, weighed on Indian equities today. Selling was concentrated in heavyweight banking and commodity stocks amid weak FII sentiment," experts noted. "Further weakness in global equities could spill over into India, though the impact may be relatively limited given India’s lower exposure to AI-driven investment and resilient domestic economy. Improving manufacturing activity and expectations of robust Q2 GDP growth of 7.7 per cent remain key fundamental supports for a constructive medium- to long-term outlook," as per analysts. ( IANS)

stories.headline: 228 GW Solar, 135.8 GWh BESS Pipeline Raise Credit & Execution Risks: Study
stories.title: 228 GW Solar, 135.8 GWh BESS Pipeline Raise Credit & Execution Risks: Study
stories.summary: Two recent reports by India Ratings and Research (Ind-Ra) and CareEdge highlight widening credit divergence among domestic solar module manufacturers amid an increasing shift towards BESS manufacturing and rising operational capacity. Demand for BESS is rising as renewable energy additions outpace transmission infrastructure development. A recent ICRA report emphasises that execution is a key monitorable in building Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) capacity amid growing storage demand and with enlarging tender pipeline. This trend is particularly acute in resource-rich states such as Rajasthan and Gujarat. This, in turn, is creating grid congestion and a growing need for storage to absorb surplus generation, shift supply to non-solar hours, and ease network constraints. India Rating and Research (IndiRa) special report, “Policy Access, Integration, and ROCE Will Drive Credit for Solar Module Manufacturers”, examines domestic manufacturing economics, ALMM-II and DCR implications, margin migration, technology and execution risks, BESS diversification, and the likely rating outlook for the sector. Emphasising on the impact on the BESS project, the research noted, a shift in Indian BESS market from tendering to execution, backed by policy support and a large tender pipeline. However, the rebound in battery prices, rupee depreciation and aggressive bids make timely battery procurement, robust LTSAs and offtake tie-ups critical for project viability. Credit Divergence & Solar Cell Import Dependence Affect the Indian Market Another key element is credit considerations, which are now emerging as an important factor requiring attention. Credit divergence across domestic solar module manufacturers is emerging in FY27, even as strong solar power demand continues, indicating widening differences in manufacturers' credit profiles. However, import dependence continues, with imported-cell modules being 3-4 US cents/W cheaper than domestic-content-requirement modules, even after basic customs duty. Consequently, the implementation of the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) List-II will be central to absorbing domestic cell capacity. The divergence is unfolding against a backdrop of stable module capacity at 228 GW, which is more than three times the estimated annual requirement of 65-70 GW. This makes capacity utilisation, technology relevance, customer access, liquidity, and returns on capital more important than announced capacity alone. Solar to Push for Further Upstream Manufacturing From Modules to Cells and Ingots Ind-Ra marks the shift in Indian solar sector with the change in its margin pool from modules to cells. With margins likely to move further upstream towards ingots and wafers as backward integration gathers pace, its expected to favour well-capitalised integrated manufacturers. However, substantially higher capex, technology, commissioning, power, and refinancing risks will increase rating sensitivity. Therefore, the winners according to the report would be those who can provider low-debt module manufacturers with strong channels and high asset turns. This may remain viable at lower margins, while leveraged greenfield projects and standalone assemblers dependent on spot cells will be more exposed as domestic cell spreads normalise. “Policy access and integration will increasingly determine market position, but neither guarantees stronger credit quality. As manufacturers move upstream, the ability to preserve return on capital, manage technology transitions, and fund expansion without weakening liquidity will separate sustainable business models from capacity-led growth,” says Bhanu Patni, Director, Corporate Ratings, Ind-Ra. BESS Pack Costs Remain Central to Assessment At a battery pack cost of USD 70/kWh, a cumulative DSCR of 1.17-1.27 times is expected at tariffs of Rs. 2.60-2.80 lakh/MW/month. Competitive procurement and protection against cost escalation remain central to the assessment. Operational BESS capacity is also rising, signalling progress from tendering to deployment. Policy support, including the Government of India’s VGF schemes announced in 2023, 2025, and 2026, covering 135.8 GWh, provides a significant source of capital support. Battery procurement costs and currency movements remain critical to the viability of aggressively bid projects. ICRA’s sensitivity analysis highlights limited coverage headroom at lower capacity tariffs. Merchant BESS Viability: Arbitrage Margins Need Adequate Utilisation Sustained arbitrage margins and adequate utilisation are critical to merchant BESS viability. ICRA’s analysis indicates a cumulative DSCR of 1.35-1.52 times at a charging cost of Rs. 2/unit and discharge realisation of Rs. 6.0-6.5/unit, under the stated assumptions. Narrowing peak-off-peak spreads, fewer viable trading cycles, lower efficiency, and availability shortfalls remain key risks to cash flows and debt coverage, necessitating adequate liquidity buffers. Lower upfront funding and supplier guarantees do not eliminate future costs and operating risks. The report reccomends project assessments to take into account eventual duty payments under Manufacturing and Other Operations in Warehouse Regulations ( MOOWR) and check whether supplier guarantees adequately cover commitments to the power buyer. Costs not covered by the supplier, including performance penalties, additional batteries, and post-warranty maintenance, remain important risks for the developer.

stories.headline: Right to correct electoral roll entry is personal, can't pursue in PIL: SC
stories.title: Right to correct electoral roll entry is personal, can't pursue in PIL: SC
stories.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday dismissed a PIL seeking corrections to municipal electoral rolls in Uttar Pradesh over discrepancies in house numbers. A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said it was not inclined to entertain the plea. "The right to seek correction of an electoral-roll entry is personal to the individual voter and cannot ordinarily be pursued collectively through a PIL. The municipal electoral rolls are governed by their own rules, and individual voters can approach the competent election authorities for corrections," Justice Bagchi orally observed. The petitioner had argued that house numbers had changed, representations remained unaddressed and municipal electoral rolls should be aligned with those used for parliamentary and Assembly elections.

article_sentences: "Stop acting like a Baahubali", the Supreme Court on Monday (November 23, 2026) remarked while slamming a Bihar judicial officer who convicted a Superintendent of Police (SP) for disobeying directions to register an FIR and fined him.
A Bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana questioned Bihar Judge Anil Kumar's conduct and said his understanding of law is appalling.
"We are really surprised at your understanding of law.
You must first understand the scope and ambit of Section 384 BNSS and Section 345 CrPC.
If someone slaps someone or abuses the court, or refuses to leave the courtroom when directed, that is an offence committed in the face of the court.
But if we direct someone to register an FIR and they do not, it does not amount to a crime committed in the face of the court.
"Your understanding of law is appalling.
You also took such an aggressive stance, called the superintendent and convicted him on the same day," Justice Bagchi remarked orally.

Questioning the Judge's objection to an inspecting Judge's intervention, Justice Bagchi said, "Were you within your domain and jurisdiction when you called the District Magistrate and Superintendent of Police, treated their non-appearance as an offence committed in the face of the court and convicted and sentenced him?
You also stay your hands.
Enough of adventure."
The SC said the judicial officer should be sent to the National Judicial Academy for training.

event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The West Bengal Government has approached the Supreme Court challenging a Calcutta High Court order deferring the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) elections until a pending challenge to the delimitation of municipal wards is decided.
A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana heard the matter on Friday.
Solicitor General Tushar Mehta appeared for the State Government.
After hearing the SG for some time, the bench adjourned the hearing till another day.

The challenge before the Supreme Court arises from a November 6 order passed by a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court, which restrained the West Bengal State Election Commission from proceeding with the KMC elections until the pending challenge to the ward delimitation exercise is finally decided by a single judge.
The dispute concerns the West Bengal Government's decision to increase the number of wards in the Kolkata Municipal Corporation from 144 to 209 ahead of the municipal elections.
The State Government issued a delimitation notification on September 11, 2026, redrawing the boundaries of the municipal wards.
The exercise was challenged before the Calcutta High Court on the ground that it was undertaken without a valid recommendation from the elected Municipal Corporation.

The petitioners questioned the authority of Smita Pandey, who had been appointed Administrator of the KMC after the elected Corporation ceased to function, to make the recommendation for delimitation.
They argued that an Administrator could not substitute the elected Municipal Corporation for the purpose of making such a recommendation.
The petitioners also alleged that the redrawing of ward boundaries amounted to gerrymandering intended to give an electoral advantage to a particular political party.
A single judge of the High Court had earlier declined to stay the delimitation exercise.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Monday made absolute its January 15 order restraining the Tamil Nadu government from taking any coercive action against SASTRA University in Thanjavur over 31.37 acres of government land allegedly encroached upon by the institution.
A bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana listed the plea of SASTRA University for final hearing.
The bench took note of the statement made by senior advocate Jaideep Gupta, appearing for the Tamil Nadu government, that the state did not want to resolve the case amicably and wanted its land back.
He also sought early listing of the petition for final hearing after the state government files its reply.
The court asked the state government to file its response to the university’s plea.

Senior advocates Mukul Rohatgi and Abhishek Singhvi, appearing for the university, said SASTRA was willing to offer an alternative piece of land, but the state government did not want to resolve the dispute.

On September 21, the top court had asked the Tamil Nadu government to explore whether suitable alternative land could be accepted in lieu of the 31.37 acres allegedly encroached upon by the university.
Observing that the land was being used for an educational institution serving a public purpose, the bench also questioned the state’s insistence on eviction and demolition of the institution.
Earlier, the bench had said that the state can identify an alternative site for its proposed open-air jail and have the university bear the cost of acquiring comparable land.

The observations came during the hearing of SASTRA University’s plea challenging the Madras High Court’s January 9 order upholding the state government’s rejection of its request for assignment or exchange of government land and directing its eviction.
The university had submitted that it had offered three parcels of alternative land to the state government but had not received an effective response.
It said the state had initially shown an inclination towards a contiguous parcel measuring 86.8 acres but later changed its position.

stories.headline: Gold snaps 10-day losing run, rises Rs 1,500 to Rs 1.26 lakh/10gm
stories.title: Gold snaps 10-day losing run, rises Rs 1,500 to Rs 1.26 lakh/10gm
stories.summary: New Delhi, Nov 23: Gold prices snapped a 10-session losing streak, climbing Rs 1,500 to Rs 1.26 lakh per 10 grams in the national capital on Monday on local demand and strong global trends. The yellow metal of 99.9 per cent purity appreciated by Rs 1,500 to Rs 1,26,800 per 10 grams (inclusive of all taxes) from Saturday's close of Rs 1,25,300 per 10 grams, according to local traders. Silver also rebounded by Rs 2,000 to Rs 1.57 lakh per kg from Rs 1.55 lakh per kg in the preceding session. "Gold prices moved higher on Monday, tracking gains in global markets and expectations of improved jewellery demand amid the ongoing wedding season," said Saumil Gandhi, Senior Analyst of Commodities at HDFC Securities. The recent correction has brought prices to more attractive levels for consumers, while seasonal buying interest is expected to strengthen as the wedding season advances, Gandhi said. A similar improvement in physical demand was reported in India and China last week, reflecting renewed consumer interest after the price decline, he added. According to Akshat Siddhant, Lead Quant Analyst at investment platform Mudrex, lower domestic prices have also drawn bargain hunters back to physical gold. A marginal weakening of the rupee also supported prices. In international markets, spot gold gained USD 84.27, or 2.38 per cent, to USD 3,622.38 per ounce, while silver appreciated by 3.3 per cent to USD 42.59. "Gold has rebounded by over 2 per cent to near USD 3,630 per ounce after a 9 per cent weekly fall to a 14-month low, as traders pared December Fed rate hike bets after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned against overtightening," said Siddhant. Jateen Trivedi, VP Research Analyst - Commodity and Currency, LKP Securities, said market participants would focus on key US economic releases, including inflation and GDP data, which could provide fresh cues on inflation, economic growth and the Federal Reserve's future interest-rate trajectory. Looking ahead, volatility in bullion is likely to remain elevated amid movement in dollar and global economic developments, he added.

stories.title: Kashmir must heed Nepal's warning, protect fragile Himalayas: Mirwaiz on Sheshnag lake excavator video
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 23: Mirwaiz-e-Kashmir Dr Moulvi Mohammad Umar Farooq on Monday expressed concern over reports of heavy machinery being used near Sheshnag Lake in the glacial zone of Pahalgam, questioning the ecological impact of construction activities in the fragile Himalayan region. In a post on X, Mirwaiz said visuals and reports of heavy machinery operating near the lake were disturbing and had raised serious concerns among people about the environmental impact of such activities. He said retreating glaciers and recent devastating glacier-related floods in neighbouring Nepal were reminders of the growing vulnerability of the Himalayan region. Mirwaiz said Kashmir had always warmly welcomed pilgrims undertaking the Amarnath Yatra and that improving facilities for them was not an issue, but stressed that such development should not come at the cost of the fragile ecosystem. "Those governing owe answers to people for the serious environmental concerns created by such 'developmental projects'!" he said. Calling for an immediate halt to the reported activities, Mirwaiz said the mountains, glaciers and water bodies needed protection for present and future generations. "Our precious mountains, glaciers and water bodies need protection not plunder, for now and for the future generations. So this must be immediately stopped," he said. The statement comes amid concerns raised by political leaders over purported visuals circulating on social media that allegedly show heavy machinery being used near Sheshnag Lake for construction work along the Amarnath Yatra route.

stories.headline: India to include data as an asset in GDP calculations in next base revision: MoSPI
stories.title: India to include data as an asset in GDP calculations in next base revision: MoSPI
stories.summary: The proposed changes are part of a broader statistical overhaul covering national accounts, household income measurement and district-level economic estimates
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Government ministries across the board are focusing on ensuring greater transparency and wider availability of data, Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) Secretary Saurabh Garg said on Monday, outlining upcoming structural shifts in how India measures its economy.

Speaking to the media on the sidelines of the Data Users Conference on the New Series of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), Consumer Price Index (CPI), and Index of Industrial Production (IIP), organised in collaboration with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), Garg stated that central departments are actively working to make granular information accessible to the public.
“I think both the Ministry of Panchayati Raj and the Ministry of Housing are working on this.
You might be aware there’s already a Panchayat Advancement Index which is published annually and which has a lot of granular information of the status of each Panchayat,” Garg noted.
“Similarly, the Ministry of Housing also has developed a portal in which a lot of these accounts are being published.
So I think all ministries are focusing on this work to ensure that there is greater transparency and availability of data,” he added.
A key pillar of the ministry’s upcoming statistical overhaul involves integrating digital information directly into national accounting.

Referring to the digital transformation sparked by the Digital India initiative in 2015, Garg explained that India is now a data-rich nation and will soon reflect this in its headline economic metrics.

“The fact that the system of national accounts 2025 focuses on data as an asset is something the mechanics, the details are being worked out and when the next base revision is done, we’ll have data as an asset as an integral part of calculation of the GDP,” the Secretary said.
